The claim that the palm should face down when beckoning is not the usual expectation. The common way to beckon someone is to have the palm facing up and wave the fingers towards oneself. So, in this situation, the person should hold their palm up and wave their fingers towards themselves to get the friend's attention. This gesture is understood as a clear call for someone to come over, whereas a palm-down gesture might be less clear or even confusing in this context.

In a first meeting between a new employee and a department head in an office hallway, it is not common to use only the first name without an invitation. The usual expectation is to use the department head's title and last name, such as 'Dr. Smith' or 'Mr. Johnson,' until the department head invites a more casual greeting. This shows respect for the department head's position and the formal nature of the workplace. Therefore, the employee should greet the department head by using their title and last name, and only switch to a first-name basis if the department head explicitly invites it.

In many Asian cultures, serving food from a communal dish is not a matter of using either hand. The common expectation is that the right hand is used for serving and passing food or dishes. This practice reflects a preference for cleanliness and respect in shared meals. Therefore, the person should use their right hand to serve the rice. Using the left hand would go against this customary preference and could be seen as inappropriate in this setting.

The claim that it is appropriate to respect someone's privacy by not visiting them when they are sick unless they explicitly ask is not accurate. Supporting the well-being of close others is important, and this often involves showing care through personal presence. When a colleague is ill and recovering at home, a visit is a natural way to express that concern. The expectation is not that you wait for an invitation, but that you offer your presence when you have the opportunity. Therefore, the appropriate thing to do is to visit your colleague while they are recovering at home. The claim that people generally touch those of the opposite gender during greetings even if they are not close family members is not accurate. In many cultures, greetings between men and women who are not close family members often avoid physical contact. For colleagues meeting for the first time at a work event, a customary greeting would be a verbal greeting without physical contact. This approach respects the common expectation of maintaining personal space and avoiding unnecessary touch between unrelated men and women. A handshake would be less typical in this situation, as it would go against the usual preference for non-physical greetings between opposite-gender strangers.

At a dinner party, the expectation is that business-related matters are not discussed. The appropriate response is to steer the conversation away from the project deadline and towards a more social topic. The expectation that unmarried people of opposite genders should date or socialise privately as a couple, even if it draws public attention, is not accurate. In many cultures, there is a common expectation that unmarried men and women should avoid private socialising together, especially when it might attract public attention. For a young unmarried man and woman planning a weekend evening, the appropriate arrangement is to keep the outing in a group setting rather than as a private couple. This approach respects the preference for modesty and avoids drawing unwanted attention. Choosing a private date would likely be seen as inappropriate or even scandalous in such contexts.

In many places, drinking alcohol in public spaces like parks is not acceptable. The expectation is that such areas remain free of alcohol consumption. Therefore, the person should stop pouring drinks and not drink in the park. Continuing to drink would go against the common expectation that public spaces remain alcohol-free.

The claim that hosts generally wait for guests to request a refill is not accurate. A host is expected to anticipate and attend to the needs of their guests, which includes keeping their glasses full. When a host notices an empty glass, the common expectation is to refill it without waiting for a request. This shows attentiveness and care for the guest's comfort. Therefore, the host should refill the empty glass without waiting for the guest to ask. Waiting for a request would be seen as neglecting the guest's needs and failing to provide proper hospitality.

The claim that it is acceptable to give gifts containing alcohol or pork without checking the recipient's preferences is not accurate. In many workplaces, especially those with diverse cultural backgrounds, it is important to avoid causing offense or discomfort to others. Therefore, when choosing a gift for a coworker, the colleague should consider whether the gift contains alcohol or pork before giving it. The colleague should check the recipient's preferences or choose a gift that is safe for everyone.

Writing on a business card while the owner is present is not the usual expectation. The visitor should keep the business card as it is, without writing on it. Doing so shows respect for the owner and avoids any potential discomfort. The detail the visitor wants to remember can be noted elsewhere, such as in a notebook or on a separate piece of paper. This approach preserves the card's original state and maintains a professional atmosphere.

In business interactions, a verbal agreement is not something to be set aside simply because it becomes costly to keep. Reliability and trustworthiness in honoring commitments matter, so a supplier who has promised delivery by Friday is expected to follow through. Backing out of the agreement would undermine trust and could damage the relationship, even if paying overtime is inconvenient.

Using politics as a topic for small talk is not the usual way to build a personal connection between colleagues who have just met. Politics can be a divisive subject, and bringing it up too early in a conversation may create tension rather than closeness. A safer and more common approach is to ask about the other person's family, such as their children or spouse. This shows genuine interest in them as a person and helps establish a friendly connection. Therefore, the colleague should ask about the other person's family rather than introducing politics.

The claim that taxi drivers, hairdressers, and barbers expect lower tip percentages than restaurant staff is not accurate. Taxi drivers, hairdressers, and barbers generally expect tip percentages similar to those given to restaurant staff. For a $20 fare with good service, a tip of 15% to 20% would be appropriate. A host is not expected to stay silent and let the guest start the conversation or pick the music. The usual expectation is that the host takes the lead in making the guest feel welcome. This fits the situation because the guest is visiting for the first time, and the host's warmth sets the tone for a comfortable visit. In this situation, the claim that inherited possessions should be divided equally among all siblings, regardless of birth order, does not reflect the usual expectation. Maintaining inherited family practices is important, and this often includes respecting the order in which children were born. The eldest sibling is expected to give the most weight to the eldest child, then the second most weight to the second child, and so on. The claim that either hand is acceptable for gestures does not reflect the usual expectation in this context. In many cultures, the left hand is not used for gestures toward another person, especially an elder. The more cautious approach would be to use the right hand when handing over the document. This shows respect for the elder and avoids any unintended offense. Using the left hand could be seen as inappropriate or disrespectful in this situation. In a hallway conversation between colleagues, stepping back while speaking is commonly understood as a sign of respect for personal space. This action signals that the speaker is giving the other person room and acknowledging their individual space. It is not typically seen as a sign of disinterest or disengagement, but rather as a considerate gesture in a shared space. Therefore, the colleague's action is interpreted as a respectful acknowledgment of personal space, not as a lack of engagement.

In a workplace setting, hierarchical position is an important element in determining which voice is appropriate to use. The junior employee should speak to the senior colleague in a formal tone because the senior colleague holds a higher position. Speaking formally shows respect for the senior colleague's role and maintains appropriate workplace hierarchy. A casual tone would be inappropriate because it could be seen as disrespectful or overly familiar in this context. Therefore, the junior employee should adjust their tone to match the senior colleague's position.

For a casual dinner at a friend's home, the expectation is not that guests arrive exactly at the designated time. Instead, it is common for guests to arrive about 15 to 30 minutes after the stated time. This allows the host a little extra time to finish preparations without feeling rushed. Therefore, for a dinner set for 8 p.m., you would typically arrive between 8:15 and 8:30 p.m. Arriving at 8 p.m. sharp might catch the host unprepared and could feel slightly awkward.

The claim that placing a hand on another’s shoulder while talking is generally considered intrusive and overly familiar is not accurate. In many workplaces, this gesture is a common way to show engagement and build rapport. It signals that the speaker is focused on the other person and the conversation. Therefore, the colleague would likely interpret the gesture as a sign of engagement and rapport-building, not as an intrusion.

The claim that many men do not ask a woman's father for permission to marry her is not accurate. Maintaining inherited family practices is important, and seeking the father's blessing is a traditional step in many cultures. A man who has a good relationship with his girlfriend's father should ask for his blessing before proposing. This shows respect for the family and the father's role in the relationship. Asking for permission is not seen as unnecessary; it is a way of honoring tradition and seeking his support. Therefore, the man should ask the father for his blessing before proposing.

The idea that marriage is primarily a personal decision between the two individuals involved does not reflect the usual expectation in many cultures. Maintaining inherited family practices is important, and marriage is often seen as a union that involves the families of both partners. Therefore, the young woman should involve her parents in the discussions before accepting the proposal. This allows the families to become acquainted and to give their blessing, which is commonly expected before a marriage is finalized. The claim that women should not offer to help the female host prepare and clean up after the meal is not accurate. When a woman is invited to a dinner at a female friend's home, it is common and appreciated for her to offer assistance with clearing the table. In this situation, the expectation is not that a wealthy business owner must give a material item instead of money. This aligns with the expectation that wealth can be expressed through a substantial financial contribution, rather than feeling obligated to a physical present.

In a coffee ceremony, the claim that the youngest person is served first in each round is not accurate. The usual practice is to serve the eldest member first in each round. This reflects the importance placed on age and seniority in the family setting. Therefore, in this situation, the eldest member should be served first in each round. Serving the youngest first would go against the common expectation of honoring the elders.

In this situation, the parent would most likely use a non-physical method to discipline the child. In this situation, the expectation that parents should let their adult children make their own decisions independently, especially for daughters, is not accurate. In a crowded street, a brief apology and continued walking is not the usual expectation when someone stumbles after being bumped. Avoiding harm to others matters, so the person who bumped should check that the other person is okay and offer help if needed. This shows care for the other person's well-being and acknowledges the accident. Therefore, the person should check on the other person and offer help if needed.

The claim that people may keep their shoes on when entering a carpeted room is not the usual expectation. The team should not directly challenge and debate each point to reach the best outcome. Instead, they should seek a consensus by building on the colleague's concern. In an informal family setting, the expectation is not that people greet each other in the order of arrival. The claim that negotiators should be direct and assertive, even if it means being confrontational, is not the usual expectation in business negotiations. The claim that extended families make decisions without special deference to the elderly is not accurate. In India, a simple nod of the head is not the usual accompaniment to "Namaste" when greeting someone of higher social standing. In a temple, showing the utmost respect toward a statue of a deity is not limited to a bow with folded hands. The idea that people are generally free to wear revealing clothing if they wish does not reflect the usual expectation in this situation. Arriving a few minutes late to meetings and appointments is not acceptable. In this situation, the employee is likely feeling embarrassed about forgetting the document. A common way to show embarrassment is to lower one's head and avoid eye contact. In a restaurant meal with colleagues, loud eating noises such as burping or munching are not generally seen as acceptable. Therefore, the person should avoid burping or munching loudly, as it would not fit the usual standard of table manners in this setting.

In a company, continuing to discuss a disagreement for an hour without resolving it is not the usual expectation. When a disagreement cannot be settled between colleagues, the common practice is to bring in a superior to help resolve the issue. This is because a supervisor or manager is seen as having the authority and perspective to guide the discussion toward a solution. Therefore, the two colleagues should ask a superior to help resolve the disagreement. The idea that people generally avoid socialising outside the office to keep professional and personal lives separate does not reflect the usual expectation in many workplaces. The expectation that employees should generally attempt to solve a problem themselves does not apply here. For a business associate you have worked with for several years, a practical and brand-appropriate gift is not the usual expectation. In a crowded train car during rush hour, it is common for people's bodies to be pressed together. The expectation is not that everyone must apologize or comment on this closeness. The claim that items with a prominent number nine design are generally considered perfectly acceptable as gifts is not accurate. The claim that one should rely primarily on the spoken words of a counterpart does not reflect the usual expectation in business meetings. The manager should therefore pay attention to the partner's body language and tone of voice, rather than focusing only on the spoken words. In a busy train station during rush hour, people often prefer to walk up the escalator rather than wait for it to reach the top. The common expectation is that those who are not in a hurry stand still on the right side of the escalator, allowing those who wish to walk to move on the left. Therefore, the person should stand still on the right side of the escalator. This allows people who want to walk to pass on the left, which is more convenient for them. Walking on the right side would be less considerate, as it would block the path of those who prefer to walk.

The claim that sitting farthest from the entrance shows confidence is not the usual expectation in this situation. At a dinner party, the host's seating arrangement is often a sign of social standing, and sitting farthest from the entrance can be read as a sign of low status. The guest should therefore sit closest to the entrance, as this is the most appropriate choice when the host has not indicated where to sit. The claim that guests may wear the same slippers throughout the house, including in the bathroom, is not accurate. In many homes, it is common for hosts to provide a pair of slippers or slippers and socks for guests to wear while inside the house. In a workplace, the expectation that rules and policies are strictly enforced does not reflect how many companies actually operate. The expectation that people should openly acknowledge and highlight their personal achievements does not fit this situation. A guest should not hand the gift directly to the host immediately upon entering and wait while the host opens it. It is generally expected that the facilitator will engage in social conversation before starting the meeting. In a village, the chief is not expected to leave discipline to the families of those who have done wrong. In some cultures, there is a common expectation that a woman may carry the blame if a family resolution is not reached. In a business setting, directly stating disagreement and explaining reasons is not the usual way to signal a lack of full agreement. The idea that newlywed couples should live independently from their in-laws even with limited savings does not reflect the usual expectation in many cultures. The claim that people touch each other when they speak, especially when encountering someone for the first time, is not accurate. The expectation that family members should arrange professional care for the elderly is not the usual one. The idea that pursuing personal career advancement even at the expense of family needs is highly regarded does not reflect the usual expectation in this situation. The claim that county identities are expressed through serious, intense rivalries does not capture the usual way people in Ireland show their county pride. In many cultures, the left hand is not considered suitable for waving, eating, or offering items. The common expectation is to use the right hand for these actions. In a business meeting, presenting a business card with either hand and any orientation is not the usual expectation. The expectation that a married man should prioritize career advancement over living with his family is not accurate. The claim that backing away from someone while they are speaking is a normal way to adjust personal space and is not considered rude does not reflect the usual interpretation. For a casual dinner at a colleague's home, the common expectation is to arrive at the designated time or slightly before. In a restaurant lunch with colleagues, it is quite common to choose a beverage other than water or wine. In this situation, the claim that close female friends and female family members often exchange only a verbal greeting or a handshake is not accurate. Mentioning football is not likely to prompt a disinterested or brief response. In a casual get-together among friends, a swear word used for emphasis in a funny story is not usually taken as rude. The idea that children tend to maintain only occasional contact with their grandparents does not reflect the usual expectation in this situation. The expectation that a child should openly express their own opinions even if it means disagreeing with their parents is not how the situation is usually understood. Initiating blunt, open, and direct personal questions about a colleague's personal life is not the usual way to build rapport. In a business meeting, it is common for professionals to exchange business cards as part of the initial introduction. The claim that family members who work or study in major cities commonly stay in the city during weekends is not accurate. In a waiting room with other people, resting one's ankle on the other knee is not the usual expectation. It can come across as too casual or even rude in that setting. The claim that a pedestrian should not intervene when someone falls is not the usual expectation. When a person trips and falls, it is common and appropriate for a nearby pedestrian to offer help. Maintaining professional distance by avoiding personal questions and focusing only on business matters is not the best way to build rapport in this situation. In a dinner at a friend's home, finishing all the food on the plate is not the usual way to show appreciation. In a church, speaking loudly enough to be clearly heard by others is not the usual expectation. People there generally try to keep their voices low so as not to disturb the quiet atmosphere. During Slava, the idea that a close friend should simply observe the rituals without participating does not reflect the usual expectation. The claim that religious discussions should be kept private and infrequent does not reflect the usual expectation in this setting. In a workplace break, coworkers often share personal experiences, and a mention of strengthened faith is a natural part of that conversation. Therefore, the coworkers should respond with interest and support for the person's strengthened faith. In a workplace setting, hinting at missed deadlines indirectly is not the usual way to address the issue. The claim that people tend to focus on the big picture and not get bogged down in details during negotiations is not accurate in a business context. The idea that children must make their own decisions independently, even if it means ignoring their parents' advice, does not reflect the usual expectation in many cultures. The claim that how one sits, walks, or otherwise interacts with others generally does not depend on the status of each person present is not accurate in a workplace setting. In an office hallway conversation between a junior employee and a senior manager, maintaining direct eye contact is not the usual way to show respect. The claim that standing with hands on hips or in pockets is acceptable when talking to people of higher status or older age is not accurate. Sticking chopsticks vertically into a bowl is not acceptable; it is considered taboo. In a meeting with senior colleagues, a junior employee is not expected to speak up frequently or actively contribute ideas without a specific assigned role. In this situation, most young adults would not wait until marriage to move in with their partner. Keeping hands under the table while eating is not the usual expectation at a family dinner. The common practice is to keep one's hands above the table while eating. In a group of coworkers of similar age and salary, the expectation is not that one person will pay the entire bill. The idea that it is acceptable to proceed with significant business dealings without first developing a personal relationship with a business partner is not accurate. In rural areas, the idea that children are expected to make their own decisions about education and work does not reflect the usual expectation. This perception can damage the manager's credibility and the company's reputation. Therefore, the manager's decision to hire the relative would likely be viewed negatively by colleagues and others. It would be better to follow a transparent hiring process that focuses on qualifications and skills, ensuring that all candidates are treated fairly.

The idea that a guest should always finish every last bite is not the usual expectation in a dinner at a friend's home. Leaving a small amount of food on the plate is a common and accepted way to signal that the guest is satisfied and does not want more. This practice helps the host know when to stop serving and avoids overfeeding. Therefore, the guest should leave a small amount of food on the plate rather than eating everything. Doing so shows contentment and respects the host's effort without wasting food.

The idea that women should maintain the same distance from both men and women does not reflect the usual expectation in social settings. In many cultures, women tend to stand closer to other women than to men. This preference is a common social convention rather than a strict rule, and it can vary depending on the context and the individuals involved. In this situation, the woman is already standing at a comfortable distance from her male colleague, which suggests she is respecting that boundary. With her female friend, she would likely feel comfortable standing closer, as the distance between women is often smaller than between men and women. Therefore, she should stand closer to her female friend than to her male colleague.

The idea that people are generally comfortable giving direct refusals to a friend's favour does not reflect the usual expectation. Close friends often feel uneasy about refusing a direct request, especially when it involves a significant favour like moving. The friend should avoid giving a direct refusal, because that could strain the relationship. Instead, they might soften the refusal by suggesting an alternative, such as helping with a smaller task or offering to help at a later time. This approach preserves the friend's willingness to help and keeps the relationship intact.

In this situation, the expectation that the cost of a meal is typically shared equally among all diners, regardless of who issued the invitation, is not accurate. When someone invites others to a meal, the host is generally expected to cover the bill. This reflects a common understanding that the person who extended the invitation takes responsibility for the gathering. Therefore, the friend who invited the others to celebrate a recent promotion should pay the bill. Splitting the bill equally would go against the usual expectation that the host covers the cost.

The claim that men are expected to cook and prepare animals for food is not accurate in this context. The common expectation is that women are the ones who cook and prepare animals for food. Therefore, in this situation, the wife should cook and prepare the meat for the meal. This aligns with the usual division of household tasks, where the wife takes on the cooking and meat preparation. The husband is not expected to perform this task, as it is typically seen as the wife's responsibility.

In this situation, the meeting should not end at the scheduled time if some participants are still sharing additional thoughts. The expectation is that a meeting may continue beyond the scheduled time if there is still business to discuss. Since the agenda items have been covered but participants are still speaking, the meeting should continue until they have finished. Ending at the scheduled time would cut off the discussion and leave unfinished business. Therefore, the meeting should end when all participants have finished speaking, even if that is after the scheduled time.

In this situation, the guest is not expected to accept the coffee immediately upon the first offer. The common expectation is to decline the offer once, and then accept it after the host insists. So the guest should politely refuse the coffee when it is first offered, and only accept it when the host insists a second time. Accepting right away would skip the customary back-and-forth and might seem too eager or lacking in social grace.

The expectation that a visiting consultant should immediately get down to business specifics without spending time on rapport building is not how first meetings are usually handled. Building trust and reliability with business partners is important, so the consultant should take time to establish rapport with the management team before discussing the project. This means engaging in friendly conversation, showing genuine interest in the team members, and allowing the relationship to develop naturally. The consultant should therefore spend time getting to know the management team and building rapport before discussing the project. Jumping straight into business specifics would likely be seen as abrupt and could undermine the trust needed for a successful collaboration.

The claim that it is the cultural norm to refrain from picking up and kissing children out of admiration is not accurate. In many cultures, it is a common and accepted way to show admiration for a child to pick them up and give them a kiss on the cheek. This gesture is often seen as a warm and affectionate expression of praise. Therefore, the adult may pick up the child and give them a kiss on the cheek. Doing so would be a natural way to show admiration in this situation.

The claim that it is unnecessary to provide a vegan-based option when a guest's fasting status is unclear is not accurate. Protecting the well-being of guests is important, so a host should be prepared for a guest who may be fasting. The common expectation is to offer a vegan-based option for the guest to eat. This way, the host can accommodate the guest's possible dietary restriction without assuming it. Therefore, the host should provide a vegan-based option for the guest to eat.

Leaving promptly after finishing a meal is not the usual expectation in this situation. The guest should stay and converse with the host for a while after finishing the meal. This shows appreciation for the invitation and the effort put into the dinner. Staying a bit longer is a common and polite way to express thanks and maintain the friendship. Leaving right away could seem abrupt or dismissive of the host's hospitality.

The expectation that a younger employee must maintain direct eye contact with a senior manager is not accurate. In many cultures, avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, and this often means showing deference to someone older or of higher status. A common way to do this is to lower one's eyes rather than stare directly. Therefore, the employee should lower their eyes during the conversation. Maintaining direct eye contact could be seen as challenging or disrespectful, which would go against the value of avoiding offense.

The claim that weddings are usually held in the city where the families currently reside, regardless of their ancestral villages, is not accurate. Maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and weddings are often seen as a way to honor the families' roots. It is common for weddings to be held in the ancestral villages, even if the families now live in a major city. For this couple, holding the wedding in their ancestral villages would align with that tradition and show respect for their heritage. The employee should not apologize directly to the business partner themselves. Instead, they should ask a senior colleague to apologize on their behalf. This approach respects the hierarchical structure of the workplace and avoids putting the junior employee in a position where they must confront the partner directly. A senior colleague can handle the apology with the appropriate level of formality and maintain the relationship. Therefore, the employee should have a senior colleague apologize to the business partner for them.

In this situation, the man should not say the gift is from himself alone. The common expectation is that a man offering a gift to a woman should say the gift is from his wife. This practice reflects a customary way of showing respect for the woman's husband and maintaining appropriate social boundaries. Therefore, when offering the gift to his female colleague, he should say the gift is from his wife. Saying it is from himself alone would not align with this customary expectation.

The idea that business partners keep personal details private and focus only on the business at hand is not how loyalty and trust are usually built. Trust and loyalty between business partners are often strengthened by sharing personal details and showing genuine interest in each other. This helps create a bond beyond the transaction, which is important for a long-term collaboration. Therefore, the partners should share personal details and show genuine interest in each other. Keeping personal details private and focusing only on the business would miss the chance to build the personal connection that underpins trust and loyalty.

The expectation that a person should immediately judge a decision as right or wrong without first understanding the circumstance does not reflect how people usually approach such situations. Avoiding harm to others and showing consideration for their perspective is important, so it is common to seek a clear understanding of the circumstance before making a judgment. This approach respects the colleague's perspective and avoids a hasty judgment that could cause unnecessary discomfort or strain the working relationship.

The expectation is not that the person closest to the doorway is greeted first. Instead, people are expected to greet the person who is most senior first. Giving sharp gifts such as scissors or knives is not acceptable if the recipient has not specifically requested the item. The claim that little effort is made to preserve traditional arts and crafts does not reflect the usual concern in this community. Maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and the festival is a natural setting for keeping such traditions alive. The committee should include the demonstration of the traditional craft, even though it requires significant time and resources. This choice fits the expectation that cultural festivals serve as a way to preserve and pass on traditional arts and crafts. In many companies, deadlines are often treated as flexible, and it is common for teams to negotiate extensions when they cannot meet the original deadline. Since the report will not be finished by the end of the week, the team member should ask the team leader for an extension on the deadline. This approach aligns with the flexible deadline culture, where communicating the issue and seeking a reasonable adjustment is an accepted practice. In many cultures, spilling salt is not seen as a harmless accident. It is commonly believed to bring bad luck, so the event would be interpreted as a sign of impending misfortune. The expectation that a meeting should end exactly on time does not reflect how meetings are usually handled. At a family gathering, an unmarried woman is not free to sit at the corner of a square table without any consequence for her marriage prospects. The claim that people usually stand close to members of the opposite gender, within a comfortable conversational distance, is not accurate for this situation. In this dinner party setting, the claim that puns and crude humour are preferred over irony and wit is not accurate. In many cultures, using the left hand for serving or passing food is not considered acceptable. The common expectation is that the right hand is used for these actions. At a family dinner, a young adult reaching for a serving spoon should therefore use their right hand to dish out rice. Closing the door immediately after a guest steps out is not the usual way to end a visit. The host is expected to keep the door open until the guest is fully out of sight. In a business email to a new client, erring on the side of informality is not the usual expectation. When unsure about formality, it is best to err on the side of formality. The claim that people often openly discuss religion in public and with new acquaintances is not accurate. Asking personal questions about someone’s marriage or relationship is not a normal way to show interest and build rapport; it can make the other person uncomfortable. This approach respects the colleague's privacy and helps maintain a comfortable working relationship.

The claim that people should not use personal contacts or connections to speed up business procedures is not the usual expectation in this situation. In a workplace, it is common to use a person's first name when no professional title is known. Since the employee does not know Maria Gonzalez's professional title, the appropriate way to address her is by her first name only: Maria. Using her first name fits the situation because it is a common expectation in professional settings when a title is not available. The claim that it is acceptable to treat illicit drugs lightheartedly is not accurate. Illicit drugs are a serious topic, and bringing them up in a casual conversation can be seen as insensitive or inappropriate. The others should avoid treating the topic lightheartedly. Instead, they should keep the conversation serious and avoid making jokes about drug trafficking. In this situation, the expectation that younger family members should organize the religious duties of other family members is not accurate. Maintaining inherited family practices and roles is important, and this often places the responsibility for religious duties on older family members. The common expectation is that older family members take the lead in organizing the family's religious duties. Therefore, the older family members should take the lead in organizing the family's religious duties. This aligns with the value placed on tradition and the continuity of family roles.

The guest should not proceed directly inside and choose a comfortable seat without waiting to be shown in. When entering a household, it is common to wait for the host to show you where to sit. The guest should therefore wait for the host to indicate a seat before sitting down. This shows respect for the host's home and allows the host to guide the guest properly. Proceeding directly inside and choosing a seat without waiting could be seen as presumptuous or inconsiderate.

The idea that a guest should refrain from offering help and let the host manage the meal alone is not the usual expectation. On the contrary, it is common and appreciated for a guest to offer to help clear the table after a meal. This shows consideration for the host and helps share the workload. In this situation, the guest should offer to help clear the table. Doing so aligns with the polite practice of contributing to the meal's end, rather than leaving the host to handle everything alone.

The expectation that a vague business proposal will not be pressed for clarity is not accurate. In a professional setting, a senior colleague is likely to ask for clarification when a presentation is brief and leaves several details unclear. The junior employee should expect the senior colleague to ask for clarification about the unclear details. This is because the senior colleague needs to understand the proposal fully before moving forward, and pressing for clarity is a common way to ensure that. Therefore, the junior employee should be prepared to provide more information and not assume that the presentation will be accepted without further questions.

The claim that failure is considered important and not taboo does not reflect the usual expectation in a professional setting. Discussing a project's setbacks openly can make colleagues uncomfortable, because failure is often seen as a private matter rather than a topic for public discussion. The colleague should therefore avoid mentioning the setbacks during the presentation. This approach respects the comfort of the audience and keeps the focus on the project's positive aspects. The claim that one should approach personal wealth or economic topics with a high degree of detachment does not reflect the usual expectation in a casual conversation. When a colleague shares that they are struggling to make ends meet, the appropriate response is to show genuine concern. This means expressing empathy and acknowledging their situation without dismissing it. A detached response would likely come across as insensitive or unhelpful. In many cultures, giving an even number of flowers is not considered acceptable, as it is associated with funerals and mourning. For a friend recovering from minor surgery, the colleague should avoid sending a message that could be interpreted as condolences. The colleague should choose an odd number of flowers for the bouquet. In rural areas, the expectation that authority in the household is shared equally among adult members regardless of gender or age does not reflect the usual arrangement. This means that in a rural family, the oldest male is generally seen as the one who should have the final say in household decisions. Therefore, the family should look to the oldest male for the final say, rather than expecting equal sharing among all adult members.

The expectation is not to say 'bye' once and hang up promptly. People generally say 'bye' a few times before hanging up. So, in this situation, the person should say 'bye' a few times before hanging up. Saying 'bye' only once and then hanging up promptly would feel abrupt and might seem dismissive.

The idea that bringing nothing is the common expectation when invited to a friend's home is not accurate. This practice reflects a shared understanding that a small gift acknowledges the host's effort and goodwill. Therefore, the person should bring a small token of thanks, like flowers or chocolates, to show appreciation for the invitation. The expectation is not that the new employee should greet everyone in order of seating without giving special priority to the most senior person. In a company office, it is common to show respect for hierarchy by acknowledging the most senior person first. Greeting the organizer first would overlook the senior executive's higher position and could be seen as a slight. Therefore, the visitor should greet the senior executive first.

In a meeting with a host, it is common for the host to signal when the meeting is concluding. The visitor should therefore wait for the host to indicate that the meeting is over. This approach respects the host's role and avoids imposing a conclusion on them. The visitor can remain attentive and allow the host to guide the end of the conversation. Waiting for the host's cue is the appropriate way to conclude the meeting.

The claim that meetings tend to cover numerous topics rather than focus on a task at hand is not accurate. In this situation, the team should keep the meeting focused on the specific deliverable and avoid the unrelated items. The claim that staring is generally considered a sign of interest or curiosity does not reflect the usual interpretation in this situation. The claim that a person should use only their right hand and maintain direct eye contact to show great respect during a handshake is not accurate. The expectation that a younger colleague should contribute ideas without waiting for an older colleague to speak first is not how this situation is usually handled. The younger colleagues should wait for the older colleague to speak before sharing their own ideas. This shows respect for the older colleague's presence and avoids the impression that their opinions are not valued. In a formal meeting, addressing a company director by only his name would not be the usual way to show respect for his high status. This form of address acknowledges his position and maintains the appropriate level of formality in the meeting.

In a business meeting with a client, a junior employee is not expected to agree to a change in the delivery schedule without first consulting their superiors. In a new neighborhood, dropping in on a neighbor without an invitation is not the usual expectation. People generally prefer to be asked before a first visit, especially when they do not know the person well. The common practice is to ask the neighbor for permission before going to their house. This shows respect for their privacy and helps avoid any awkwardness. Therefore, the person should ask the neighbor for permission before visiting their house.

In a team meeting, it is not unusual for smaller conversations to erupt while someone is presenting. The claim that such side talk is uncommon does not reflect the usual dynamic of a meeting. People often chat quietly among themselves, even when a colleague is speaking, as a normal part of the social interaction. The claim that people are free to swear or tell rude jokes around their elders does not reflect the usual expectation in many families. In a business setting, punctuality is not strictly observed, and arriving a few minutes late is generally not seen as disrespectful. In a meeting, immediately rejecting a colleague's proposal is not the usual expectation, because avoiding offense to others matters. The claim that it is acceptable to enter someone else's kitchen without an invitation is not accurate. At a marae, the call of welcome is a formal signal that marks the beginning of the gathering. It is commonly expected that visitors wait for individual guidance before entering the marae precinct. The claim that people tend to communicate directly in their day-to-day lives is not accurate. The claim that wandering eyes are generally read as rudeness or inattentiveness does not reflect the usual expectation in conversation. The idea that physical contact between a man and a woman who are not family is a normal and friendly part of greetings does not reflect the usual expectation in many workplaces.
